belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

Let’s begin with the business case. The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It is what earns the project its support. People outside the team only back what they can understand and size — and it is the first thing the Define report shows.

Here’s an illustration of a completed business case: “During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month.”

Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves time and resources, showing what is wrong, where and since when, how big the issue is today, and what it costs.
reply.example: “During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month.”
reply.prompt: Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.

Now let's move on to the project team. 

The project team is the group of people who will actively work on solving the problem. It includes the leader (you, Priya), the champion (a sponsor who clears obstacles), and the process owner (the person responsible for keeping the improvements in place after the project ends). It also includes any other team members who contribute their expertise, and notes if anyone needs training to participate fully.

Why does the team matter? A project needs people before it needs work. The champion clears obstacles and the process owner ensures that the solution sticks after the project ends. Without these roles clearly defined, even the best improvement can fade.

Here’s an illustration of a completed team description:
- Leader: Anna (Green Belt, runs the project).
- Champion: Mark, Finance Director (approves, removes blockers).
- Process owner: Jo, Billing Manager (owns the process).
- Members: two billing clerks (know the work).
- Training: the clerks need a half-day on data collection before Measure.

Who leads the project? Who is the champion who can approve and clear obstacles? Who owns the process? Who else is on the team — and does anyone need training to take part fully?

Let's move to the Voice of the Customer (VOC) and Critical-to-Quality requirements (CTQs).

**What it is:** The Voice of the Customer captures who receives the outputs of your process — inside the company, outside, or both — what they need, and the Critical-to-Quality requirements (CTQs) that turn those needs into measurable terms.

**Why it matters:** It keeps the project honest. We improve what matters to the people receiving the output, and a CTQ is how "they want it accurate" becomes a requirement you can check.

**Illustration (not your data):** Customers: client finance teams (external) and our credit control (internal). They need invoices that are correct and on time; the top complaint is wrong amounts. CTQs: invoice amount matches the agreed price on 100% of lines; invoice sent within 2 working days of the order.

**Ask:** Who are the customers of your process, and what do they need or complain about most? For each need, how would you measure that it is met?
reply.explanation: The Voice of the Customer identifies who receives the process outputs, what they need, and how those needs translate into measurable requirements (CTQs).

problem_5w2h.why: Interest, lost discounts, and supplier stops.
problem_5w2h.how: Suppliers chase us by phone and email, and some put us on stop.
problem_5w2h.how_much: 23% of invoices were paid late over January to June 2026 — one measure, the late payment rate.

define_structured.baseline_estimate: One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.

metric_definitions.name: late_payment_rate
metric_definitions.meaning: The share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date.

project_scope.in_scope: Invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites.
project_scope.out_scope: Non-PO invoices, payroll, procurement tendering, and the ERP system itself.

define_structured.goal_statement: Reduce the late payment rate from 23% to under 5% by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.
